results.title: 🇰🇵🇨🇳 North Korea and China are close because it serves both of their interests, but in reality Kim Jong-un is not all that fond of China.
results.description:
🇰🇵🇨🇳 North Korea and China are close because it serves both of their interests, but in reality Kim Jong-un is not all that fond of China. That's because Kim knows full well that China has long been waiting for its chance to swallow up North Korea. 

So on August 20, 2026, when Lee Jae-myung met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the presidential office in Seoul that morning, Kim Jong-un fired more than ten short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea around 5 p.m. the same day, just about an hour and a half after Wang Yi left South Korea. 

This was no coincidence. Lee Jae-myung is a fake president of South Korea, elected through election fraud by the Chinese Communist Party, and he is trying to hand South Korea over to China wholesale. 

If Lee succeeds in handing South Korea to China, North Korea will be isolated and surrounded by the CCP, and it will only be a matter of time before North Korea falls to China as well.

What Kim Jong-un wants most is not to be merged with China. He wants to preserve his regime. That's why he occasionally shows a willingness to talk with the United States: it's a way to keep China in check. If he grew too close to China, it would become far easier for China to have him killed, and North Korea would be absorbed into China. The missile launch a few months ago was not the first time Kim has shown wariness of a South Korean president cozying up to China. 

On September 15, 2021, when former South Korean President Moon Jae-in, another prominent Chinese spy much like Lee Jae-myung, met Wang Yi in Seoul that morning, North Korea fired two ballistic missiles toward the East Sea at 12:34 p.m. and 12:39 p.m., right after Wang Yi's meetings had wrapped up.

So what should we do when we hear that Kim Jong-un's health is in danger? The free democratic world must keep its eyes wide open and watch closely for any move by China to swallow North Korea. Even without taking South Korea, China would find it far easier to reach the Pacific simply through North Korea's rivers. This would be especially effective for an invasion of Japan, and from there China could advance to the U.S. mainland across the open Pacific. And once China controls North Korea, it would share a border with South Korea, making it much easier to take the South than it is now.

That's not all. The upside-down "east-up" map of Korea that USFK Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson unveiled on November 17, 2025, clearly shows why China covets North Korea, South Korea, and the Korean Peninsula so much. Korea is a geopolitical linchpin of Asia, and taking Korea would make it far easier for China to seize global hegemony.

In his article on the USFK website, Gen. Brunson wrote, "Perhaps the most significant insight from east-up mapping is the emergence of a strategic triangle connecting Korea, Japan, and the Philippines," noting that Korea "provides strategic depth and central positioning within the regional architecture, with the added advantage of cost-imposition capabilities against both Russian and Chinese forces."

🇰🇷 The best outcome Koreans hope for is this: 
to remove Lee Jae-myung, a puppet of the Chinese Communist Party, from the presidency by having his election declared invalid; to restore President Yoon Suk Yeol, who truly cherishes liberal democracy; to strengthen the alliance with the United States; and then to reunify the Korean Peninsula under liberal democracy, led by South Korea. 

When that happens, the North Korean regime, a member of the axis of evil, will disappear for good, and the Republic of Korea will become an even stronger liberal democracy in Asia, a powerful pillar of the free world that holds back the Chinese Communist Party's influence right on its doorstep, and a nation able to contribute greatly to the security of free democracies around the world.

results.title: U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said Wednesday the Korea-U.S. alliance is going through "turbulence." She called it part of a
results.description:
U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said Wednesday the Korea-U.S. alliance is going through "turbulence." She called it part of a move toward a stronger, more equal partnership.

Speaking at an AMCHAM event in Seoul, Steel urged South Korea to "stand up and lead together with the United States" in the Indo-Pacific. She called China "the greatest threat in the Indo-Pacific region."

She also said U.S. companies in Korea "deserve to compete on a level playing field," citing searches, audits and fines against American firms. She did not name any company.

Is Seoul ready to take on a bigger leadership role in the alliance?

Source: Yonhap, SBS

results.title: U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said: “South Korea is no longer a country that simply relies on U.S. protection.” She criticiz
results.description:
U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said: “South Korea is no longer a country that simply relies on U.S. protection.”

She criticized the lack of a level playing field for American companies, pointing to raids, audits, and fines in the digital sector, and described the relationship as “turbulence.”

This goes beyond protecting U.S. firms. 

Under the Lee Jae-myung administration, pressure linking the Coupang case to intelligence sharing and security talks has grown, and Steel is openly pushing South Korea to move from being protected to sharing the burden.

If U.S. deterrence weakens, the costs of dealing with China and North Korea will fall more directly on South Korea. Her remarks are essentially a call to reallocate that burden.

Source: KBS
